name: Shungite Pyramid
subtitle: Shungite, cut to an 8cm x 8cm pyramid
standfirst: Shungite - a carbon-bearing stone, cut and polished into an 8cm x 8cm pyramid here. It comes from the Karelia deposits in north west Russia, and it's a stone, not a supplement: no dose, no ingredients list, just the mineral itself, eight centimetres at the base.
body: Shungite comes out of a group of deposits in Karelia, close to Lake Onega, in the far north west of Russia. The rock formed in the Precambrian, something like two billion years back, laid down as organic sediment then buried, heated and pressed until the carbon in it locked solid. It's one of the oldest carbon-bearing rocks we know of, and one of the few places on earth where that carbon sits in a workable stone, rather than as coal or graphite.

The stone itself is black, dense and a little greasy under the fingers once it's polished, closer to graphite in feel than to a crystal. It cuts and takes a shine well, which is why it gets worked into pyramids, spheres and jewellery rather than left as raw rubble. This piece is an 8cm x 8cm pyramid, four faces polished to a low sheen.

Shungite is also one of the small number of natural minerals known to carry fullerenes, carbon molecules that include C60, in trace amounts. That's a genuine, documented feature of the rock's chemistry. It's a fact about what the stone is made of, not what it does once it's sitting in a room.
spec: Karelia, north west Russia, near Lake Onega
Precambrian, estimated at around two billion years old
Contains naturally occurring fullerenes, including C60, in trace amounts
dose: Not applicable. It's a stone, not a food supplement, and it isn't taken by mouth.
supply: One pyramid, one to an order.
cautions: Not a food supplement, and not for ingestion.
Keep it away from small children. A stone this size and weight is a choking and an impact hazard.
Polished stone chips if it's dropped on a hard surface. Handle it the way you'd handle any dense mineral piece.
imageSubject: A black polished shungite pyramid, 8cm at the base, photographed against a plain neutral surface, showing its dark lustre.
queries: No weight is given for this pyramid on the current listing. Can Reiss supply it so the spec sheet is complete.

The live listing doesn't state a carbon grade or percentage for this pyramid, unlike the Elite Noble Shungite Stone (99%) or the Water Stones (99%). Is this the same high-carbon grade, or the more common lower-carbon shungite typically used for larger carved pieces? That single fact would materially change what we can say about it.

Removed claim: the live listing describes the stone as providing antioxidant support, restoring electron balance, protecting cells and reducing oxidative stress, and enhancing wellbeing. All of this has been removed as unauthorised health claim language.

name: Lion's Mane
subtitle: Hericium erinaceus, vegan capsules
standfirst: Hericium erinaceus - the shaggy white bracket fungus known as lion's mane, encapsulated here on its own, no fillers added. The current listing doesn't print a capsule count, a capsule weight or an extraction method, so this page holds to what's confirmed and leaves the rest as a question.
body: Hericium erinaceus grows out of the wounds of hardwood trees, mostly beech and oak, right across the temperate forests of the northern hemisphere. It doesn't fruit as a cap and stem at all, it fruits as one cascading mass of long white spines, and that's where every one of its names comes from: lion's mane, bearded tooth, monkey head, pom pom mushroom.

The listing describes Herbase's capsules as 100% Hericium erinaceus, no fillers, no bulking agents, no contaminants. What it doesn't say is whether the mushroom used is fruiting body, the fungus itself, grown on logs or substrate and harvested directly, or mycelium grown on grain, a cheaper and very different material that gets sold under the same name. Neither is stated on the current listing, and it's the one fact that would tell a customer what they're actually holding.

The same question sits over extraction. A capsule can be filled with plain dried powder, or with a hot water or dual extract concentrated down to a stated ratio, and the two aren't the same material at all. None of that's printed here either. A beta-glucan percentage, the figure most labels use to show how much of the mushroom's structural material actually made it into the capsule, is missing too.
spec: Lion's mane, bearded tooth fungus, monkey head mushroom, pom pom mushroom
None stated beyond the capsule shell: described as free from fillers, bulking agents and contaminants
dose: Two capsules in the morning, with at least 500 ml of spring water.
supply: Capsule count and capsule weight aren't printed on the current listing, so we can't work out a day count here. See queries.
cautions: Always consult a healthcare professional before use, particularly if you're pregnant, nursing or on medication.
Not suitable for anyone with a known mushroom or fungal allergy.

name: Elite Noble Shungite Stone
subtitle: Noble grade shungite, approx. 20 to 30 g
standfirst: Noble shungite - the high-carbon grade of the stone, cut from the Karelia deposits in north west Russia, hand-sized here at around 20 to 30 grams. No ingredients, no dose: a mineral object, described as what it is.
body: Shungite out of Karelia varies a great deal by grade. Ordinary shungite runs somewhere between 30 and 50 percent carbon and reads dull black. The rarer grade, called noble or elite shungite, runs much higher, close to pure carbon, and carries a silvery, almost metallic lustre where the ordinary stone is matte. This stone is sold as that higher grade.

The listing states a carbon content of around 99 percent for this stone. That figure describes the proportion of the rock that's carbon, a straightforward compositional fact about a mineral, the same kind of figure you'd expect on any ore or gemstone. It isn't a description of anything the stone does once you own it.

Shungite of any grade, including this one, is also one of the few natural minerals known to carry trace fullerenes, including C60. That's a genuine feature of the rock's chemistry, worth stating plainly. Each stone weighs approximately 20 to 30 grams, small enough to sit in a pocket or a drawer.
spec: Shungite, noble or elite grade (high carbon content)
Approximately 99%, as stated by the supplier
Precambrian, estimated at around two billion years old
Contains naturally occurring fullerenes, including C60, in trace amounts
dose: Not applicable. It's a stone, not a food supplement, and it isn't taken by mouth.
supply: One stone per order, weighing approximately 20 to 30 g.
cautions: Not a food supplement, and not for ingestion.
Keep it away from small children: a stone this size is a choking hazard.

queries: Can Reiss confirm a lab assay or certificate for the 99% carbon figure, given it is now the headline compositional fact on this page?

The live listing describes the stone as '99% C60', which conflates carbon content with fullerene content. Fullerenes occur in shungite only in trace amounts, a natural stone cannot be 99% fullerene. We've written the 99% figure as carbon content and mentioned fullerenes separately without a percentage. Worth checking with the supplier which figure the 99% actually refers to.

name: Reishi
subtitle: Ganoderma lucidum, 50 vegan capsules x 800 mg
standfirst: Ganoderma lucidum - sold here as reishi, 50 vegan capsules at 800 mg each, described on the listing as 100% pure with no fillers.
body: Ganoderma lucidum is a bracket fungus that grows on the trunks and roots of deciduous trees, plum, oak and maple especially. In the wild it forms a hard, woody, kidney-shaped cap with a glossy, varnished surface, dark reddish-brown fading to cream at the growing edge. It's known across East Asia under many names, most commonly reishi in Japan and lingzhi in China, and few fungi anywhere carry as long a continuous trade history.

Herbase's capsules list the fill as 800 mg of Ganoderma lucidum, described as 100% pure, in a pack of 50 vegan capsules. What the listing doesn't say is whether that 800 mg is the whole mushroom in powdered form, fruiting body or mycelium grown on grain, or a concentrated extract at a stated ratio. It doesn't give a beta-glucan figure either. These are the facts that would actually tell a customer what grade of reishi they're buying, and none of them are on the label yet.
spec: None printed beyond the capsule shell
dose: Two capsules a day with breakfast or lunch, and at least 500 ml of spring water.
supply: Fifty capsules. At two a day, that's 25 days.
cautions: Always consult a healthcare professional before use, particularly if you're pregnant, nursing or on medication.
Not suitable for anyone with a known mushroom or fungal allergy.

name: Omega Oil
subtitle: Omega-3 oil, 6:1 ratio, 9,000 mg per tablespoon
standfirst: An oil blend formulated to a stated ratio of six parts omega-3 to one part omega-6, delivering 9,000 mg of omega-3 per tablespoon. The listing doesn't name the plant it's pressed from or confirm a DHA figure, so both sit logged as queries.
body: The listing describes this oil as rich in alpha-linolenic acid, ALA, an omega-3 fatty acid, blended to a ratio of six parts omega-3 to one part omega-6. It states a figure of 9,000 mg of omega-3 per tablespoon. What it doesn't state anywhere is which plant the oil's pressed from, flaxseed, hemp, chia or something else, and there's no separate DHA figure printed, only the total omega-3 number.

That distinction actually matters. ALA is a precursor the body converts into other fatty acids, DHA among them, but it isn't DHA itself, and a product's DHA content has to be measured and printed on its own before it says anything about DHA specifically. Until we have that figure and the source plant confirmed, this page states the ratio and the total omega-3 figure exactly as printed, and nothing more.
spec: Not printed on the current listing
Not stated on the current listing
supply: One bottle. Printed on the listing as a one month supply. Bottle volume in millilitres isn't given.
cautions: Always consult a healthcare professional before taking supplements.
Not intended to replace prescription medication.
Check the full ingredients and allergen list on the bottle before use.

queries: What plant is this oil pressed from? The listing only says it is rich in ALA and doesn't name a source, flax, hemp, chia or otherwise. This also determines whether the product is vegan, which matters given other Herbase products are marked as such.

Is there a DHA figure in milligrams per serving printed anywhere, separate from the total omega-3 figure? DHA has an authorised claim on the GB Nutrition and Health Claims Register, but only if the product delivers a qualifying amount of DHA specifically and that amount is printed. If Reiss can supply that figure, we can look at whether the authorised wording applies. We have not written that claim here.
What is the bottle size in millilitres?

Given the product doesn't appear to contain preformed DHA, only its precursor ALA, should 'DHA' remain in the product's name at all? We've named it 'Omega Oil' on this page pending an answer, dropping 'DHA' from the name until it's confirmed.

name: Anamu
subtitle: Petiveria alliacea, 50 vegan capsules
standfirst: Petiveria alliacea - sold as Anamu, 50 vegan capsules with no fillers, binders or artificial ingredients.
body: Petiveria alliacea is a shrub native to the Caribbean and South America, known too as guinea hen weed, mucura, tipi. It grows wild right across the region and sits deep in Caribbean and South American herbal tradition, most easily known by the strong sulphurous, garlic-like smell that comes off its crushed leaves and root, a smell that carries straight through into the dried, encapsulated material.

That smell comes from sulphur compounds in the plant, dibenzyl trisulphide among them, one of the compounds Anamu is best known for chemically. Herbase's capsules are 100% Petiveria alliacea, harvested from organically grown sources in the Caribbean and South America, nothing added at the encapsulation stage, no fillers, no binders, no artificial ingredients.

Each pack is 50 vegan capsules. The listing's own guidance on how long that lasts doesn't agree with itself: at one capsule a day it calls fifty capsules a forty day supply, a discrepancy we've flagged rather than repeated here.

body: Inonotus obliquus grows on living birch trees in cold climates right across the northern hemisphere, forming a hard, black, cracked mass on the trunk that looks more like burnt charcoal than a mushroom. That mass, properly called a conk or a sclerotium, is the part harvested and used, not a cap and gills at all.

Herbase's capsules list 750 mg of pure Chaga extract to a capsule, in a vegan formulation free from fillers or additives. As with the other mushroom pages in this batch, what isn't stated is whether that 750 mg is dried whole material or a concentrated extract at a given ratio, whether it's the conk itself or mycelium grown on grain, and what the beta-glucan content actually is. name: Shilajit
subtitle: Altai Mountain resin, 50 g amber glass jar
standfirst: Shilajit - a dual-extracted resin scraped from rock in the Altai Mountains, sold here in a 50 g amber glass jar. Fulvic acid and humic acid are named on the listing as compounds present in the resin.
body: Shilajit is a dark, sticky resin that seeps out of rock strata in a handful of high-altitude mountain regions, the Altai among them. It forms over long stretches of time as plant matter, trapped and pressed between layers of rock, breaks down slowly under pressure and heat into a dense organic material rich in humic substances. At bottom, it's the compressed by-product of ancient plant decay, squeezed out of the mountainside. Think of the archetype of mountains, and this reads as Capricorn, set in resin.

Herbase's resin is described as dual-extracted and lab-tested, sold in a 50 g amber glass jar. Fulvic acid and humic acid are the two named compounds on the listing, both naturally occurring humic substances typical of this kind of material rather than anything unique to this product. The listing also names a longer list of minerals present, zinc, copper, nickel, manganese, potassium, phosphorus, vanadium, chromium, cobalt and magnesium among them, though it doesn't give a lab-verified breakdown with quantities.

Because shilajit is scraped from rock rather than grown and harvested, purity testing is a real and useful question, specifically testing for heavy metals like lead, arsenic and mercury, which can occur alongside the mineral content in unrefined material from some sources. Whether this particular resin's been tested for that isn't stated on the current listing, and it's the single fact that would most improve this page.
spec: Dual-extracted, lab-tested, as stated on the listing
Zinc, copper, nickel, manganese, potassium, phosphorus, vanadium, chromium, cobalt, magnesium, without stated quantities

dose: A pea-sized portion, dissolved in 300 to 500 ml of warm spring water, taken once daily in the morning, or morning and evening.
supply: One 50 g jar. Printed on the listing as approximately a two month supply.
cautions: Always consult a healthcare professional before use.

Material scraped straight from rock can carry heavy metals if it isn't properly tested and purified. Ask to see a certificate of analysis before use if you've any doubt.
